subject: St Antony (Anthony) the Great, also called Antony of Egypt and Anthony the Abbot

text_used.text: Quotations from the Life of Antony are checked against H. Ellershaw's unrevised translation (NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892, ed. Archibald Robertson), downloaded whole from CCEL as plain text and saved as sources/people/antony-the-great/athanasius-life-of-antony-npnf204.txt. 'exact' is the translation as printed, footnote numbers taken out. 'display' applies the site's rule of capitals for every pronoun for God. Sayings of the Desert Fathers are checked against Budge's 1907 translation from the Syriac (Wikisource transcription and the archive.org scan). Other texts: see each item.
text_used.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony, tr. H. Ellershaw, NPNF2-04 (1892), CCEL, marked Public Domain
text_used.note: The CCEL plain text drops most OPENING quotation marks (it prints `For,' said he, the fibre...'`), so quotations were matched ignoring quote marks and the right marks restored from New Advent. New Advent (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/2811.htm) is a REVISED copy of the same translation: it modernises hath/has, wroth/angry and similar. The site's quiz lines mix the two (the 'anger' line uses the CCEL 'wroth', the 'effort' line uses New Advent's 'has'). Pick one edition for the page; the CCEL chapter pages (npnf204.xvi.ii.*) carry the unrevised text, like Martin's page. Chapter links: each CCEL page was fetched (HTTP 200) and mapped to its chapters (e.g. .iii = chapters 1-2, .xi = the sermon, chapters 16-43, .xxxiii = chapters 72-79). The Life was written between 356 and 362 (Robertson's introduction in the same volume).

born_year.text: About 251. The Life gives no year, but says he was 'near a hundred and five years old' when he died, and he died in 356.
born_year.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 88, editor's footnote (E. C. Richardson, NPNF2-03): 'Born 251, died 356'; OCA life ('in the year 251'); Great Synaxaristes (synaxarion.gr: 'Ημ. Γέννησης: 251 μ.Χ.'); Coptic Synaxarium, Toba 22 ('born in the year 251 A.D.'); Britannica ('born c. 251'); Life of Antony, chapter 89 ('near a hundred and five years old')
born_year.note: 251 is worked back from 356 and '105'. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) says only 'about the middle of the third century'. Merriam-Webster's biographical entry says 'circa 250-355'.

born_place.text: Born at Coma, a village in Middle Egypt, to a Christian family of good standing. The Coptic Church and the Monastery of St Antony name it Qimn al-Arous (Qiman al-Arus), near Beni Suef.
born_place.source: Life of Antony, chapter 1 ('Antony you must know was by descent an Egyptian: his parents were of good family and possessed considerable wealth, and as they were Christians he also was reared in the same Faith'); Sozomen, Church History, Book 1, chapter 13 ('He was an Egyptian by race, and belonged to an illustrious family of Coma, which was situated near the Heraclea which is on the Egyptian borders'); Coptic Synaxarium, Toba 22 ('in the city of Qimn El-Arouse'); Monastery of St Antony ('born in Qimn al-Arus, near Beni Suef')
born_place.note: The Life itself does not name the village; Sozomen (about 440) does. Sources differ on where Coma lay: the Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) 'near Heracleopolis Magna in Fayum'; the Great Synaxaristes 'Κομὰ τῆς Ἄνω Αἰγύπτου, κοντὰ στὴ Μέμφιδα' (near Memphis); Britannica 'Koma, near Al-Minyā'. Heracleopolis and Beni Suef agree; Britannica's Al-Minya is the outlier. Safe wording: 'Coma, in Middle Egypt (today Qiman al-Arus, near Beni Suef)'. New Advent's page 26021 is titled 'Book II' but holds Book 1 (it contains chapter 13).

grew_up.text: At home in his village, with his Christian parents. He would not learn letters, and did not care to mix with other boys. He went to church with his parents and listened closely to the readings.
grew_up.note: Exact: 'he could not endure to learn letters, not caring to associate with other boys; but all his desire was, as it is written of Jacob, to live a plain man at home.' Augustine (On Christian Doctrine, Preface) says he could not read and 'is said to have committed the Scriptures to memory through hearing them read by others'. CHECKER 2026-09-25: 'play with other boys' and 'go to school' went beyond the source ('not caring to associate with other boys').

died.text: 356, in his 'inner mountain' in the desert near the Red Sea, where the Monastery of St Antony stands today. He fell ill in old age, a few months after saying goodbye to the monks of his 'outer mountain'. He was about 105.
died.source: Life of Antony, chapters 89 and 91 ('after a few months he fell sick'); Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 88, footnote ('died 356'); Catholic Encyclopedia 1907 ('St. Jerome places his death in 356-357'; the monastery 'Der Mar Antonios' on the mountain near the Red Sea); OCA ('died peacefully in the year 356, at age 105')
died.note: Day: 17 January is the day the churches keep, and Britannica gives 'died January 17?, 356' with a question mark. No ancient text I read gives the day. The Coptic Synaxarium puts his death on 22 Toba 'of the year 355 A.D.'. The mountain is Mount Colzim (Qulzum): Monastery of St Antony page ('Mount Qulzum'). Britannica calls the place 'Dayr Mārī Antonios hermitage, near the Red Sea'.

buried.text: By his two companions, in secret, as he had ordered, so that no one would keep his body above ground in a house, as Egyptians then did with holy men. Athanasius says no one but those two knew the place.
buried.source: Life of Antony, chapters 90-92 ('they afterward, according to his commandment, wrapped him up and buried him, hiding his body underground. And no one knows to this day where it was buried, save those two only.')
buried.note: The two are named elsewhere as Macarius and Amatas (Palladius, Lausiac History, chapter 21: 'Macarius and Amatas, who also buried him when he died'; Jerome, Life of Paul, chapter 1: 'Amathas and Macarius, two of Antony's disciples, the former of whom laid his master in the grave'). What happened to the body later is disputed: see how_he_died.later.

also_called.text: Antony the Great (Orthodox and Coptic). The OCA: 'Venerable and God-bearing Father Anthony the Great'. Greek: 'Ὁ Ὅσιος Ἀντώνιος ὁ Μέγας'. Russian: 'Преподобный Антоний Великий, Египетский'.
also_called.note: Sozomen already calls him 'Antony the Great' (Church History 1.13, heading and text). azbyka.ru says he 'earned the name the Great' for his labours ('за свои подвиги заслужил наименование Великого').

also_called.source: USCCB readings page, 17 January 2026: 'Memorial of Saint Anthony, Abbot' (read through the Wayback Machine copy of 25 January 2026; usccb.org itself answered 403)
also_called.note: Also 'Anthony Abbot' in Western art titles.

also_called.source: Church of England Common Worship calendar ('Antony of Egypt, Hermit, Abbot, 356'); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 ('Antony of Egypt, Monastic, 356'); Evangelical Lutheran Worship ('Antony of Egypt, renewer of the church, c. 356')

also_called.text: Father of all monks (Coptic): 'the star of the wilderness, and the father of all monks'.
also_called.note: The OCA also: 'known as the Father of monasticism'.

also_called.text: 'The man of God', what the crowds at Alexandria called him; 'God-beloved', what his village called him as a young man; 'the great one', what the monks called him.
also_called.source: Life of Antony, chapter 70 ('We ask to see the man of God,' for so they all called him') and chapter 4 ('used to call him God-beloved'); Palladius, Lausiac History, chapter 21 ('While the great one is still alive'----for so they called Antony')

status.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and the Coptic Church. The Church of England keeps him as a Lesser Festival, and the Episcopal Church and the ELCA remember him. The Missouri Synod's calendar (Lutheran Service Book) does not list him.
status.source: USCCB; 1916 Roman Martyrology; OCA; synaxarion.gr; copticchurch.net; Church of England; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; ELW; CPH list of LSB commemorations
status.note: The CPH list (LSB pages xii-xiii) for January: Loehe (2), the Cappadocians (10), Sarah (20), Chrysostom (27), with no Antony. goodshepherd.nb.ca's LSB calendar agrees.

patron_of.text: Britannica: 'a patron saint of Christian monasticism, butchers, gravediggers and cemeteries, basket makers, brush makers, and animals', and 'invoked against the disease of ergotism (also known as St. Anthony's fire)'. The Greek synaxarion lists him as patron (πολιούχος) of the town of Veria (Βέροια) in Greece.
patron_of.source: Britannica, 'St. Anthony of Egypt'; Great Synaxaristes (synaxarion.gr: 'Πολιούχος: Βέροιας')
patron_of.note: Britannica gives 'basket weavers' in one place and 'basket makers' in another. The 1916 Roman Martyrology's list of patrons has no entry for him, and the Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) names no patronage. His feast is often kept with a blessing of animals (Britannica: 'an annual blessing of livestock near St. Peter's Basilica').

in_art.text: In the West: an old bearded monk with a T-shaped staff (the tau), often with a pig and a small bell. The pig and bell are not from his life: they come from the medieval Hospitallers of St Anthony, who rang bells as they collected alms and whose pigs were allowed to run free in the streets.
in_art.source: Britannica ('The bells of the Hospitallers, as well as their pigs ... became part of the later iconography associated with St. Anthony'); Catholic Encyclopedia 1907, 'Orders of Saint Anthony' (the Antonines 'wore a black habit with the Greek letter Tau (St. Anthony's cross) in blue')
in_art.note: Lippi's panel (the band picture) shows the T-shaped staff with prayer beads.

in_art.text: The Temptation of St Anthony: demons attacking him, a favourite subject for Bosch, Grünewald, Ernst, Cézanne and Dalí, and for Flaubert's novel.
Meeting Paul the Hermit, with a raven bringing bread (e.g. Velázquez). This comes from Jerome's Life of Paul, which the Catholic Encyclopedia says 'cannot be used for historical purposes'.
in_art.source: Jerome, Life of Paul the First Hermit, chapter 10 (the raven); Catholic Encyclopedia 1907

in_art.text: In Eastern icons: a monk in a dark hood marked with a cross and a brown cloak, with a long white beard, holding a staff and an open scroll.
in_art.source: The two icons examined here (Dionysiou icon; Cretan icon already on the site)
in_art.note: Observed from the pictures only. No reference work checked for Eastern iconographic rules.

wrote.text: Seven letters, in Coptic, sent to monasteries, according to Jerome, who knew them in Greek translation. Whether the surviving letters are his is debated. He did not write in Greek, and he spoke through an interpreter to Greek speakers.
wrote.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 88 (Richardson, NPNF2-03): 'sent seven letters in Coptic to various monasteries, letters truly apostolic in idea and language, and which have been translated into Greek. The chief of these is To the Arsenoites.' Catholic Encyclopedia 1907: the seven 'may be authentic, but it would be premature to decide'; the Sermons and twenty Arabic epistles are 'by common consent pronounced wholly spurious'; 'St. Anthony knew no Greek and spoke only Coptic'. Palladius, Lausiac History 21: Cronius 'was blessed Antony's interpreter in these conversations, since he does not know Greek'. Life of Antony, chapters 72 and 74: he spoke to the philosophers 'by means of an interpreter'.
wrote.note: Modern scholarship (Samuel Rubenson, The Letters of St. Antony, 1990/1995) is widely reported to accept the seven letters as genuine: NOT checked here. No public-domain English of the letters was found. Count to print: 7, with 'Jerome says'.

pronounced.text: AN-thuh-nee, or AN-tuh-nee (chiefly British, and the usual way to say the spelling 'Antony'). Merriam-Webster gives \ˈan(t)-thə-nē\, chiefly British \ˈan-tə-\ for 'Anthony, Saint, circa 250-355, Egyptian monk'.
pronounced.note: Google rewrites 'antony the great' to 'anthony the great' (SEARCH-BRIEF), so print both spellings: 'Antony (Anthony) the Great'.

roles.text: Heir: at about 18 to 20 he heard one Gospel verse and gave his family's land to the villagers.
Hermit: first near his village and in the tombs, then nearly twenty years shut in a ruined fort across the Nile.
Father of monks: from about 305 he guided the monks who settled around him, and 'the desert was colonised by monks'.
roles.source: Life of Antony, chapters 14-15; Catholic Encyclopedia 1907 ('about the year 305')
roles.note: The year 305 is the Catholic Encyclopedia's and Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022's ('In 305, he left his cave'), not the Life's.

roles.text: Friend of the martyrs: at Alexandria in the persecution of 311 he served the confessors in the mines and prisons.
roles.source: Life of Antony, chapter 46 (the persecution 'under Maximinus'; NPNF heading 'Persecution (311)')

roles.text: Elder of the inner mountain: his last forty-odd years, near the Red Sea, where emperors wrote to him.
roles.source: Life of Antony, chapters 49-50, 81; Catholic Encyclopedia 1907 ('the last forty-five years of his life')

catholic.text: 17 January, a memorial in the General Roman Calendar ('Memorial of Saint Anthony, Abbot'). The 1916 Roman Martyrology has him on 17 January too.
catholic.source: USCCB, readings for 17 January 2026 (Wayback copy of 25 Jan 2026); The Roman Martyrology (1916), 17 January
catholic.note: 1916 Martyrology, 17 January, exact (OCR joined): 'In Thebais, St. Anthony, abbot and spiritual guide of many monks. He was most celebrated for his life and miracles, of which St. Athanasius has written a detailed account. His sacred body was found by divine revelation, during the reign of the emperor Justinian, and brought to Alexandria, where it was buried in the church of St. John the Baptist.' Copy: archive.org/details/romanmartyrology00cathuoft. The current (2004) Martyrology not checked.

orthodox.text: 17 January in the Greek churches and the OCA. The Russian Church keeps 17 January on the old calendar, which is 30 January on the civil calendar.
orthodox.source: Great Synaxaristes (synaxarion.gr, 'Ημ. Εορτής: 17 Ιανουαρίου'); OCA ('Commemorated on January 17'); azbyka.ru ('День памяти 30 января')
orthodox.note: GOARCH blocked the checker again (HTTP 403), as it did for Martin. Unlike Martin, all Orthodox sources agree on the day; only the calendar differs.

coptic.text: 22 Toba (Tobi) in the Coptic calendar: 'The Departure of St. Anthony the Great (Antonius)'. 22 Toba falls on 30 January (Gregorian), which is 17 January on the old Julian calendar.
coptic.source: Coptic Synaxarium, Toba 22 (copticchurch.net); Wikipedia 'Tobi (month)' table, citing St-Takla.org: Tobi runs 'between January 9 and February 7 of the Gregorian calendar', so Tobi 22 = 30 January
coptic.note: The Gregorian equivalent shifts by one day in some years around Coptic leap years; say 'about 30 January' or '30 January in most years'. The same day as the Russian 30 January: both keep 17 January Julian.

anglican.text: 17 January, a Lesser Festival in the Church of England: 'Antony of Egypt, Hermit, Abbot, 356'.
anglican.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar (Antony is printed in roman type, which the page's key says marks a Lesser Festival; Charles Gore on the same day is in italics, a Commemoration)

episcopal.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 (calendar and page 42)
episcopal.note: Its collect asks God to help us as He enabled 'thy servant Antony to withstand the temptations of the world, the flesh, and the devil'. That is a prayer to God about him, not to him.

lutheran.text: ELCA: 17 January, 'Antony of Egypt, renewer of the church, c. 356', together with 'Pachomius, renewer of the church, 346'. LCMS: not in Lutheran Service Book.
lutheran.source: Evangelical Lutheran Worship, 'The Church Year', final draft January 2006 (ELCA / Augsburg Fortress), Wayback copy; CPH list of LSB commemorations
lutheran.note: The ELW source is the published final draft, not the printed book. Same document Martin's page used.

why_17_january.text: Churches keep 17 January as the day he died ('the departure', Coptic). No early text gives the day: Athanasius gives no date at all.
why_17_january.source: Coptic Synaxarium ('The Departure'); Britannica ('died January 17?, 356'); Life of Antony, chapters 89-92 (no date)
why_17_january.note: Where the 17 January tradition first appears was not traced.

numbers.text: 18 to 20: his age when his parents died. Not six months later he heard the Gospel and gave his land away.
numbers.source: Life of Antony, chapter 2 ('his age was about eighteen or twenty')

numbers.text: 300: the 'acres' of good farmland he gave to the villagers. The Greek word is aroura, an Egyptian land measure of 100 cubits square, so the English 'acres' is approximate.
numbers.source: Life of Antony, chapter 2 ('three hundred acres, productive and very fair'), with NPNF footnote 991 ('arourai. The arura was 100 Egyptian cubits square')
numbers.note: An aroura is smaller than an English acre; do not convert without a source. Print '300 fields' or '300 acres, as the translation has it'.

numbers.text: Nearly 20: the years he spent shut in the ruined fort, fed with bread let down twice a year.
numbers.source: Life of Antony, chapters 12 ('received loaves, let down from above, twice in the year') and 14 ('for nearly twenty years')

numbers.text: 35: his age when he was beaten by demons in the tombs and heard a voice promise, 'I will make thy name known everywhere'.
numbers.source: Life of Antony, chapter 10 ('he was then about thirty-five years old')

numbers.text: 105: his age at death, by his own count.
numbers.source: Life of Antony, chapter 89 ('I am near a hundred and five years old')

numbers.text: 7: the letters he sent in Coptic to monasteries, according to Jerome.
numbers.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 88

numbers.text: 13: days' journey from Nitria to his mountain, the distance at which he saw the soul of Amun carried up at the hour Amun died.
numbers.note: Could go in the miracles section instead.

numbers.text: 2: sheepskins he left in his will, one to Athanasius and one to Bishop Serapion.
15: years his two companions had lived with him on the mountain before he died.
numbers.source: Life of Antony, chapter 91 ('they were two in number who had remained in the mountain fifteen years')

traits.title: cheerful and at peace
traits.text: Strangers could pick him out of a crowd of monks by his face. He was no taller or broader than the rest.

quote.exact: he was never disturbed, for his soul was at peace; he was never downcast, for his mind was joyous.
quote.display: he was never disturbed, for his soul was at peace; he was never downcast, for his mind was joyous.
quote.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
quote.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: word for word

also.exact: from the joy of his soul he possessed a cheerful countenance
also.display: from the joy of his soul he possessed a cheerful countenance
also.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
also.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: word for word

traits.title: the same after twenty years alone
traits.text: When friends broke down the door of the fort, he came out neither fat nor thin. His soul was just as even.

quote.exact: it was neither contracted as if by grief, nor relaxed by pleasure, nor possessed by laughter or dejection
quote.display: it was neither contracted as if by grief, nor relaxed by pleasure, nor possessed by laughter or dejection
quote.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
quote.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: word for word

traits.title: humble, and ready to learn
traits.text: He bowed to bishops and priests, gave way to a deacon in prayer, and asked questions of anyone.

quote.exact: he was not ashamed to bow his head to bishops and presbyters
quote.display: he was not ashamed to bow his head to bishops and presbyters
quote.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
quote.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: word for word

also.exact: if any one said anything that was useful he confessed that he was profited
also.display: if any one said anything that was useful he confessed that he was profited
also.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
also.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: word for word

traits.title: quick-witted
traits.text: Philosophers came to mock him because he had never learned to read. He asked them which comes first, mind or letters. They said mind.

quote.exact: Whoever, therefore, hath a sound mind hath not need of letters.
quote.display: Whoever, therefore, hath a sound mind hath not need of letters.
quote.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
quote.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: None
quote.note: New Advent has 'has ... has'. The research file quoted the New Advent form. New Advent's revised text words this differently (see note).

also.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
also.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: word for word

traits.title: gentle with the troubled
traits.text: A possessed young man he had prayed over all night shoved him at dawn. Those who brought him were angry.

quote.exact: Be not angry with the young man, for it is not he, but the demon which is in him.
quote.display: Be not angry with the young man, for it is not he, but the demon which is in him.
quote.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
quote.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: word for word

traits.title: unimpressed by emperors
traits.text: Constantine and his sons wrote to him. He did not want to open the letters.

quote.exact: Do not be astonished if an emperor writes to us, for he is a man; but rather wonder that God wrote the Law for men and has spoken to us through His own Son.
quote.display: Do not be astonished if an emperor writes to us, for he is a man; but rather wonder that God wrote the Law for men and has spoken to us through His own Son.
quote.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
quote.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: None
quote.note: New Advent's revised text words this differently (see note).

traits.title: fierce against heresy
traits.text: He drove Arian visitors off his mountain and went down to Alexandria to denounce them.

quote.exact: he drove them from the mountain, saying that their words were worse than the poison of serpents.
quote.display: he drove them from the mountain, saying that their words were worse than the poison of serpents.
quote.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
quote.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: word for word

traits_note: Pick 4. Sozomen's summary backs the first and fifth: 'He was exceedingly meek and philanthropic, prudent and manly; cheerful in conversation and friendly in disputations' (Church History 1.13, verified in sozomen-church-history-1-13.txt).

others_on_him.exact: And it was as if a physician had been given by God to Egypt. For who in grief met Antony and did not return rejoicing?
others_on_him.display: And it was as if a physician had been given by God to Egypt. For who in grief met Antony and did not return rejoicing?
others_on_him.note: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 quotes the same passage in a modern wording.

others_on_him.exact: For not from writings, nor from worldly wisdom, nor through any art, was Antony renowned, but solely from his piety towards God.
others_on_him.display: For not from writings, nor from worldly wisdom, nor through any art, was Antony renowned, but solely from his piety towards God.

others_on_him.exact: He was exceedingly meek and philanthropic, prudent and manly; cheerful in conversation and friendly in disputations, even when others used the controverted topics as occasion for strife.
others_on_him.display: He was exceedingly meek and philanthropic, prudent and manly; cheerful in conversation and friendly in disputations, even when others used the controverted topics as occasion for strife.
others_on_him.note: Not an eyewitness; he summarises the Life.

others_on_him.exact: speaking of Antony, the Egyptian monk, whose name was in high repute among Thy servants, though up to that time not familiar to us.
others_on_him.display: speaking of Antony, the Egyptian monk, whose name was in high repute among Thy servants, though up to that time not familiar to us.
others_on_him.note: Augustine never met him. This is the conversation with Ponticianus that led to his own conversion (Book 8, chapter 12).
others_on_him.who: Augustine, about thirty years after Antony's death

others_on_him.exact: as he himself wrote the life of the divine Antony, and set forth, in the form of a narrative, the laws of the monastic life.
others_on_him.display: as he himself wrote the life of the divine Antony, and set forth, in the form of a narrative, the laws of the monastic life.
others_on_him.source: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow (tr.), NPNF2-07 (1894)
others_on_him.who: Gregory of Nazianzus, 380, on the Life

others_on_him.exact: His doctrine surely was pure and unimpeachable; and his temper is high and heavenly, without cowardice, without gloom, without formality, without self-complacency.
others_on_him.display: His doctrine surely was pure and unimpeachable; and his temper is high and heavenly, without cowardice, without gloom, without formality, without self-complacency.
others_on_him.work: John Henry Newman, Church of the Fathers, as quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), 'St. Anthony'
others_on_him.source: E. C. Butler, Catholic Encyclopedia vol. 1 (1907)

life_moments.title: One verse
life_moments.text: Six months after his parents died, he walked into church thinking of the apostles who left everything. The Gospel being read was Christ's word to the rich young man. He went straight out and gave his family's land to the villagers. He sold the rest for the poor, keeping a little for his young sister. When he heard 'be not anxious for the morrow', he gave that away too, and placed his sister with a community of virgins.

quote.exact: Antony, as though God had put him in mind of the Saints, and the passage had been read on his account, went out immediately from the church
quote.display: Antony, as though God had put him in mind of the Saints, and the passage had been read on his account, went out immediately from the church
quote.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
quote.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: word for word

life_moments.note: Year: Robertson's introduction ('about 275?'); Catholic Encyclopedia ('about 270'). The Life gives no year.

life_moments.title: Beaten in the tombs
life_moments.text: He shut himself in a tomb, and a friend brought him bread. One night demons beat him so badly that the friend found him lying as if dead and carried him to the village church. At midnight he woke and asked to be carried back. Alone again, he saw the roof open and a ray of light come down, and the pain left him. He asked where God had been. A voice answered.

quote.exact: Antony, I was here, but I waited to see thy fight; wherefore since thou hast endured, and hast not been worsted, I will ever be a succour to thee, and will make thy name known everywhere.
quote.display: Antony, I was here, but I waited to see thy fight; wherefore since thou hast endured, and hast not been worsted, I will ever be a succour to thee, and will make thy name known everywhere.
quote.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
quote.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: None
quote.note: New Advent's revised text words this differently (see note).

also.exact: Where wert thou? Why didst thou not appear at the beginning to make my pains to cease?
also.display: Where wert Thou? Why didst Thou not appear at the beginning to make my pains to cease?
also.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
also.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: None
also.note: New Advent's revised text words this differently (see note).

life_moments.title: Twenty years in a fort
life_moments.text: He crossed the Nile and walled himself into an old fort full of snakes, with bread for six months. Bread was let down to him twice a year. Visitors outside heard voices and din inside. After nearly twenty years, friends broke the door down. He walked out looking just as they remembered him. Cells soon spread over the mountains around him.

quote.exact: he was just the same as they had known him before his retirement

life_moments.title: In his best clothes
life_moments.text: When the persecution under Maximinus came, he went to Alexandria to stand by the martyrs. He would not hand himself in, but he served the confessors in the mines and prisons. The governor ordered every monk out of the city. The others hid. Antony washed his robe and stood all the next day on a raised place where the governor would pass.

quote.exact: he washed his garment, and stood all next day on a raised place before them, and appeared in his best before the governor.
quote.display: he washed his garment, and stood all next day on a raised place before them, and appeared in his best before the governor.

life_moments.title: Further into the desert
life_moments.text: Crowds would not leave him alone. He waited by the Nile for a boat to go south where no one knew him. A voice told him to go into the inner desert instead. He travelled three days with Saracen traders to a high mountain with a cold spring and a few palm trees, and he made it his home. He grew his own grain so the brothers would not have to carry bread to him.

quote.exact: recognising it as his own home, he remained in that place for the future.
quote.display: recognising it as his own home, he remained in that place for the future.
quote.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text
quote.check: CCEL: word for word; New Advent: word for word

life_moments.note: The Monastery of St Antony stands there now (Catholic Encyclopedia 1907; the monastery's own page, 'Mount Qulzum').

life_moments.title: Against Arius
life_moments.text: The Arians claimed he agreed with them. Angry, he came down to Alexandria and denounced them in public: the Son of God is not a created being. Crowds, pagans too, ran to see 'the man of God', and many became Christians. Athanasius walked him to the city gate.

quote.exact: he denounced the Arians, saying that their heresy was the last of all and a forerunner of Antichrist.
quote.display: he denounced the Arians, saying that their heresy was the last of all and a forerunner of Antichrist.

life_moments.title: Letters from emperors
life_moments.text: The emperor Constantine and his sons wrote to him as to a father. He did not want to read the letters, saying he did not know how to answer such things. The monks talked him round. He wrote back telling them to remember the judgment to come, that Christ alone is the true King, and to be merciful and care for justice and the poor.

quote.exact: Do not be astonished if an emperor writes to us, for he is a man
quote.display: Do not be astonished if an emperor writes to us, for he is a man
quote.source: H. Ellershaw (tr.), NPNF 2nd series vol. 4 (1892), CCEL plain text

recorded.text: Yes. The Life is full of healings, visions and wonders. Athanasius insists they were Christ's work, not Antony's: he 'healed not by commanding, but by prayer and speaking the name of Christ'.

items.title: Fronto
items.text: Fronto bit his own tongue and was in danger of losing his eyes. He came to the mountain and asked Antony to pray. Antony told him to go home to Egypt and he would be healed. Fronto stayed on, and Antony said he could not be healed there. He went, and as soon as he set eyes on Egypt the illness stopped.

items.title: The girl from Busiris
items.text: A girl from Busiris in Tripolitania was paralysed and terribly ill. Her parents brought her with some monks, and waited outside the mountain with Paphnutius. Before the monks could tell Antony about her, he told them her story. He would not see her, and said God would heal her where she was. They went out and found her whole.

items.title: Polycratia
items.text: Count Archelaus asked Antony to pray for Polycratia of Laodicea, a Christian woman sick in stomach and side from too much fasting. The count wrote down the day of the prayer. When he reached Laodicea she was well. He asked when she had recovered, and showed her the paper: it was the day Antony prayed.

more.text: Crossing the desert with monks, the water ran out and all lay down to die. Antony knelt a little way off and prayed, and water welled up where he knelt.

more.text: He had to cross the Arsinoite canal, which was full of crocodiles. He prayed, went in with his companions, and all crossed safely.

more.title: Amun's soul
more.text: Sitting on his mountain, he saw a soul carried up with great joy, and a voice said it was Amun of Nitria, thirteen days' journey away. His monks marked the day. Thirty days later brothers from Nitria confirmed Amun had died that day and hour.

more.title: The wild beasts
more.text: Animals coming for water trampled his garden. He took hold of one gently and spoke to them all, and they never came near again.

more.title: A warning to a persecutor
more.text: Balacius, a general who favoured the Arians, beat virgins and flogged monks. Antony wrote warning him that wrath was coming. Balacius spat on the letter. Within five days his own quiet horse bit him and tore his thigh, and three days later he died.

misquoted_or_legend.text: Claim: 'A time is coming when men will go mad, and when they see someone who is not mad, they will attack him, saying, You are mad; you are not like us.' Shared as Antony predicting our times. What the sources say: it is in the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, a collection made long after his death, not in anything he wrote. The popular wording is Benedicta Ward's modern translation (1975) of the Greek collection. Budge's 1907 translation of the Syriac says 'silly' as well as 'mad'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, saying 179 (checked); Ward's wording not checked (copyrighted book)
misquoted_or_legend.note: Fair wording: 'a saying the desert monks remembered'. Do not call it a prophecy in our voice. CHECKER 2026-09-25: the page no longer says the popular wording is a modern translation (Ward not checked); it says the saying names no time.

misquoted_or_legend.text: Claim: prayers to find lost things ('St Anthony, please come around'; 'Tony, Tony, turn around') are his. What the sources say: those are to St Anthony of Padua, a Franciscan who died in 1231. Merriam-Webster lists them as two people: 'Saint circa 250-355 Egyptian monk' and 'Antony of Padua, Saint 1195-1231 Franciscan friar'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Merriam-Webster, 'Anthony' (entries 1 and 4); 1916 Roman Martyrology, 13 June ('At Padua, St. Anthony, a native of Portugal'); Britannica, 'St. Anthony of Padua' ('He is commonly invoked for the return of lost property'), fetched by the checker 2026-09-25
misquoted_or_legend.note: CHECKER 2026-09-25: the custom is now sourced to Britannica (sources/people/antony-the-great/britannica-st-anthony-of-padua.txt). The page must not print a prayer to either saint (house rule).

misquoted_or_legend.text: Claim: he was the first monk, or the first hermit. What the sources say: the Life itself says an old man in the next village 'had lived the life of a hermit from his youth up', and Antony learned from him. Jerome says Paul of Thebes went into the desert first. His title is 'Father of monks' because others followed him.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Life of Antony, chapter 3; Jerome, Life of Paul, chapter 1; Catholic Encyclopedia 1907 ('He probably was not the first Christian hermit'); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 ('some forms of urban monastic life (particularly for women) existed even before his call')

misquoted_or_legend.text: Claim: he was a disciple of Paul of Thebes (Britannica says so). What the sources say: Athanasius never mentions Paul. In Jerome's story Antony, already about ninety, first hears of Paul and finds him only just before Paul dies. The Catholic Encyclopedia says Jerome's Life of Paul 'cannot be used for historical purposes'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Britannica ('A disciple of St. Paul of Thebes'); Jerome, Life of Paul, chapters 7-16 ('Antony at the age of ninety'); Catholic Encyclopedia 1907

misquoted_or_legend.text: Claim: the pig and the bell show things from his life. What the sources say: they come from the Hospitallers of St Anthony, founded about 1100, whose pigs roamed medieval streets and who rang bells collecting alms.

Claim: 'On the Character of Men and on the Virtuous Life: 170 Texts', which opens the Greek Philokalia, is by him. What the sources say: its modern English translators put it in an appendix and say it is 'almost certainly not of Christian origin, but seems to be a compilation of extracts from various Stoic and Platonic writers'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: The Philokalia vol. 1, tr. Palmer, Sherrard and Ware (1979), introductory note to the piece (copyrighted; short quotation only); OrthodoxWiki, 'Philokalia'
misquoted_or_legend.note: Seen in the archive.org scan of the translation (archive.org/stream/Philokalia-TheCompleteText). Do not link that scan on the page: it is a copyrighted book.

misquoted_or_legend.text: Claim: he could not read, so he was uneducated and wrote nothing. What the sources say: Athanasius says he would not learn letters, and Augustine says he knew the Scriptures by heart from hearing them. But Jerome says he sent seven letters in Coptic, 'truly apostolic in idea and language'. He did not speak Greek and used interpreters.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Life of Antony, chapters 1, 3, 72-73; Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, Preface; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 88; Palladius, Lausiac History 21

misquoted_or_legend.text: Question people search: 'was Anthony the Great black?' What the sources say: Athanasius calls him 'by descent an Egyptian', Sozomen 'an Egyptian by race', and he spoke Egyptian (Coptic), not Greek. No early source describes the colour of his skin.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Life of Antony, chapter 1; Sozomen, Church History 1.13; Palladius, Lausiac History 21 (interpreter)

rows.note: Said to Abba Pambo. Budge numbers it 197; the Greek alphabetical collection has it as Antony 6 (not checked).

rows.statement: Wisdom is worth learning from anyone, even people who don't share your faith.
rows.line: We Christians therefore hold the mystery not in the wisdom of Greek arguments, but in the power of faith richly supplied to us by God through Jesus Christ.
rows.note: Antony to the philosophers (chapters 72-80). Same in CCEL and New Advent.

rows.statement: Anger at real wrongdoing can be a good thing.
rows.line: And once also the Arians having lyingly asserted that Antony's opinions were the same as theirs, he was displeased and wroth against them.
rows.note: Athanasius's narration. The site's line has 'wroth' (CCEL, unrevised); New Advent has 'angry'.

rows.statement: If you had to choose, you'd grow closer to God alone in quiet than among other people.
rows.line: Fishes, if they remain long on dry land, die. And so monks lose their strength if they loiter among you and spend their time with you. Wherefore as fish must hurry to the sea, so must we hasten to the mountain.
rows.note: To a military commander ('the duke') who begged him to stay. Same in both editions.

rows.statement: Nature can teach you as much about God as the Bible can.
rows.line: 'My book, O philosopher,' replied Anthony, 'is the nature of things that are made, and it is present whenever I wish to read the words of God.'
rows.place: Socrates, Church History, Book 4, chapter 23 (quoting Evagrius, Praktikos, chapter 92)
rows.check: word for word, apart from quotation marks or their spacing (the CCEL plain text drops many opening quote marks; Budge has a space before a closing quote)
rows.note: Greek of Praktikos 92 checked (Dysinger's Greek text).

rows.statement: The best way to live is free of strong emotions, with only a steady peace inside.
rows.note: Hidden on the site (no line shown).

rows.statement: Your body is a friend to look after, not an enemy to fight.
rows.line: 'For,' said he, 'the fibre of the soul is then sound when the pleasures of the body are diminished.'
rows.check: word for word, apart from quotation marks or their spacing (the CCEL plain text drops many opening quote marks; Budge has a space before a closing quote)
rows.note: Word for word in New Advent; in CCEL the opening quote marks are missing.

rows.statement: God still speaks to people through dreams.
rows.note: Hidden on the site (no line shown).

rows.statement: Miracles still happen today, just as they did in the Bible.
rows.line: For the working of signs is not ours but the Saviour's work.
rows.note: In the sermon to the monks (chapters 16-43, CCEL page .xi). The line stops at 'work'; the source continues with a colon.

rows.statement: Some questions about God are better left alone.
rows.by: as the desert monks remembered it
rows.line: Abba Joseph saith, "I do not know." And Abba Anthony said unto him, "In truth, Abba Joseph, thou hast found the way to say, 'I do not know.'"
rows.place: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Book 1, chapter 10, saying 551

rows.statement: Becoming a better person is mostly down to your own effort.
rows.line: Wherefore virtue has need at our hands of willingness alone, since it is in us and is formed from us.
rows.note: In the sermon. The site's line follows New Advent ('has need', 'has its'); CCEL has 'hath need'.

friends_family_rivals.text: Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria: his friend and biographer. Antony left him a sheepskin and the cloak Athanasius had once given him, now worn old.
friends_family_rivals.source: Life of Antony, chapter 91 ('To Athanasius the bishop give one sheepskin and the garment whereon I am laid, which he himself gave me new, but which with me has grown old'); chapter 71 (Athanasius saw him out of Alexandria)

friends_family_rivals.text: His younger sister: he placed her with a community of virgins. Years later he rejoiced to find her grown old in virginity and leading other virgins.
Serapion, bishop of Thmuis: received the other sheepskin, and was with Antony when he saw visions of what was happening in Egypt.
friends_family_rivals.note: Thmuis: OCA ('Saint Serapion of Thmuis'); the Life says only 'Serapion the bishop'.

friends_family_rivals.text: Macarius and Amatas: the two disciples who lived with him at the end and buried him.
friends_family_rivals.source: Palladius, Lausiac History, chapter 21; Jerome, Life of Paul, chapter 1
friends_family_rivals.note: Palladius places Macarius and Amatas at Pispir. The Life only says 'two'.

friends_family_rivals.text: Amun of Nitria: a founder of monastic Nitria. Antony saw his soul carried to heaven the hour he died, thirteen days' journey away. In the Syriac sayings Ammon asks why Antony is more famous though he works harder, and Antony answers, 'Because I also love the Lord more than thou.'
friends_family_rivals.source: Life of Antony, chapter 60; Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Questions and Answers, saying 180
friends_family_rivals.note: The saying names 'Ammon of Nitria'; that he is the same Amun as in the Life is likely but not stated.

friends_family_rivals.text: Paul the Simple: an old farmer who left an unfaithful wife and begged Antony to take him as a monk. Antony tested him hard for days, then made him a monk and gave him a cell.
friends_family_rivals.source: Palladius, Lausiac History, chapter 22; Sozomen, Church History 1.13

friends_family_rivals.text: Didymus the Blind, the Alexandrian scholar: Antony told him not to grieve for eyes that ants and flies have too, but to rejoice in the sight that saints and apostles have.
friends_family_rivals.source: Jerome, Letter 68, section 2 (Jerome says it happened 'in my childhood'); Socrates 4.25 ('It is said'); Sozomen 3.15

friends_family_rivals.text: Constantine the Great and his sons: wrote to him as to a father. Antony pressed Constantine to recall the exiled Athanasius; Constantine refused and told him to respect the synod's decision.
friends_family_rivals.source: Life of Antony, chapter 81; Sozomen, Church History, Book 2, chapter 31

friends_family_rivals.text: The Arians and the Meletians: he would have no fellowship with either, and on his deathbed told his disciples the same.
Balacius, a general who persecuted Christians for the Arians: Antony warned him by letter; he died days later (see miracles).
Paul of Thebes: in Jerome's story the first hermit, whom Antony found and buried with the help of two lions. Legend.
friends_family_rivals.source: Jerome, Life of Paul; Catholic Encyclopedia 1907

friends_family_rivals.text: Augustine never met him, but hearing his story in Milan about 386 moved Augustine to his own conversion: he opened Paul's letters at random, 'for I had heard of Antony'.
Hilarion of Gaza: the Syriac sayings have them greet each other as 'star of light' and 'pillar of light'. Jerome's Life of Hilarion also tells of a visit.
friends_family_rivals.source: Budge, The Paradise vol. 2, Questions and Answers, saying 112
friends_family_rivals.note: Jerome's Life of Hilarion not opened; saying 112 seen in the Budge text only.

summary.text: He visited the monks of his outer mountain one last time, told them he was near 105 and would not see them again, and returned to his inner mountain so no one would keep his body in a house. After a few months he fell ill. He gave his last words to his two companions, left his sheepskins to Athanasius and Serapion, and died looking joyful, 'as though he saw friends coming to him'.

witness.text: Athanasius was not there. The account came from the two companions.
witness.source: Life of Antony, chapters 91-92 (only the two were with him)
witness.note: Inference from the text; Athanasius does not say who told him.

later.text: Later tradition (West): his body was found 'by divine revelation' under Justinian and taken to Alexandria, then to Constantinople, then to France. The OCA gives 544 for Alexandria, the seventh century for Constantinople, and Arles in the fifteenth century.
later.note: Dates differ between sources (the Great Synaxaristes: 'Ημ. Ανακομιδής Λειψάνων: 635'; the monastery page: 527, 668, 1080). OCA writes 'a diocese outside Vienna' where it must mean Vienne in France. Treat all as later tradition.

later.text: The Monastery of St Antony (Coptic) calls the transfer 'A False Claim': it says his body still lies in a cave before the southern altar of the old church at the monastery.
later.source: Monastery of St Antony, 'Saint Anthony The Great' page
later.note: Give both claims in their holders' words; Athanasius says no one knew the place.

summary.text: Yes, in every ancient church. Catholics, Orthodox and the Coptic Church count him a saint. The Church of England keeps him as a Lesser Festival, and the Episcopal Church and the ELCA remember him. The Missouri Synod does not list him.
summary.source: USCCB; OCA; synaxarion.gr; copticchurch.net; Church of England; LFF 2022; ELW; CPH

'Venerable and God-bearing Father', 17 January (30 January on the old calendar)
A Lesser Festival in the Church of England, 17 January

not_a_martyr.text: He wanted martyrdom in 311 but was not killed. Athanasius says that afterwards he was 'daily a martyr to his conscience'. The OCA calls the Life 'the first biography of a saint who was not a martyr'.
not_a_martyr.note: Exact: 'was there daily a martyr to his conscience, and contending in the conflicts of faith' (chapter 47).

martyrology_quote.q: In Thebais, St. Anthony, abbot and spiritual guide of many monks. He was most celebrated for his life and miracles, of which St. Athanasius has written a detailed account.
martyrology_quote.note: The OCR prints the first word as 'TN' (a drop capital).

prayer_he_wrote.text: None found. No prayer of his survives in a public-domain English translation. The Life records spoken prayers (e.g. chapter 10, 'Where wert thou?'), but none written by him.
prayer_he_wrote.source: Life of Antony; Catholic Encyclopedia 1907 on his writings

groups.text: desert, monks. The hint 'desert monks' is right. He is not usually counted a Church Father (he wrote little and no theology).
groups.source: Life of Antony; Catholic Encyclopedia 1907 ('father ... of monasticism')

lived.text: 300s. Keep the hint. He was born about 251, but everything the sources tell of him as a hermit and teacher falls between about 285 and his death in 356.
lived.note: If the filter allows two values, 'pre300' could be added for his birth and early ascetic years (about 270).

side.text: east. The hint is right: he lived in Egypt, in the Greek-speaking East, though he spoke Coptic. He is honoured in West and East alike.

hearth.text: The site names him first among the Hearth's kindred ('Light-hearted, and at your best when life is quiet'): 'He spent twenty years alone in the desert. When he came out, Athanasius says, his friends were amazed at how settled he was, and his face was cheerful because his soul was at peace.'
hearth.note: Checks out, with two small stretches. (1) 'twenty years ... in the desert': the Life says 'nearly twenty years' in a ruined fort on the mountain across the Nile (chapters 12-14). (2) 'his face was cheerful because his soul was at peace' is chapter 67, a general description, not his coming out of the fort (chapter 14: 'they ... wondered at the sight'; 'altogether even'). Consider 'nearly twenty years'. Live page not opened.

watcher_line.text: Cassian names him for the Watcher line: 'as we know that in the past Elijah and Elisha, and in our own day the blessed Antony and others who followed with the same object, were joined most closely to God by the silence of solitude.'
watcher_line.source: John Cassian, Conferences, Conference 14 (Abbot Nesteros), chapter 4; site/src/data/personality.json LINE_TEXT.watcher
watcher_line.note: The site says 'Cassian names this line first'; the speaker in the Conference is Abbot Nesteros.

hard_topics.text: The devil as 'a black boy'. In chapter 6 the spirit of lust appears 'like a black boy, taking a visible shape in accordance with the colour of his mind', and Antony calls it 'black-hearted'. Modern readers find the image racially charged. Say so plainly if the page tells the tombs story; do not paraphrase it away.
hard_topics.note: Critics' words not fetched. David Brakke, 'Ethiopian Demons: Male Sexuality, the Black-Skinned Other, and the Monastic Self', Journal of the History of Sexuality 10 (2001) is the standard study; not opened. If used, quote only after checking.

hard_topics.text: A hard line on dissenters: no fellowship with Meletians or Arians, even on his deathbed; Arian words 'worse than the poison of serpents'.
hard_topics.note: Holders: fidelity to Nicaea (the OCA: 'to preserve the Orthodox Faith in its purity'). Critics: the NPNF introduction notes the Life's anti-Arian stress fits Athanasius's own cause.

hard_topics.text: Shame of the body. He ate 'with shame', never bathed or washed his feet, and wore a hair shirt to the end.
hard_topics.note: Robertson (NPNF introduction): 'Antony's shame of the body is not in the spirit of the writer ad Amunem' (citing Gwatkin); the Budge sayings have Antony warn that monks who 'vex their bodies' without understanding 'are remote from the path of God' (saying 296).

hard_topics.text: Whose Antony? Almost everything comes from one bishop with a cause. The Life presents him as unlettered, obedient to clergy and fiercely anti-Arian; the seven letters (if his) show a more learned thinker.
hard_topics.source: NPNF2-04 introduction (Robertson): 'even an Athanasius would not so entirely rise out of the biographical habits of his day as to mingle nothing of his own with the speeches of his hero'

site_data_flags.text: people.antony.hook: 'He spent the next eighty years in the desert'. From about 20 to 105 is about 85 years, but his first fifteen or so were near his village and in the tombs; he reached the desert fort at about 35 (chapters 3, 8-12). The OCA does say 'Saint Anthony spent eighty-five years in the solitary desert'. Consider 'the rest of his long life'.
The quiz lines mix two editions of the same translation: 'anger' follows CCEL ('wroth'), 'effort' follows New Advent ('has need'). Harmless, but a page that also quotes the Life should pick one.
The site's portrait credit dates the Cretan icon '15th to 17th century'; its Commons page gives no better date.
site_data_flags.note: Commons page not reopened in this pass.

site_data_flags.text: The research file (group-05) calls Sozomen's 'Coma' and Budge sayings 'nos. 2-3' correctly; its Syriac saying numbers all check. Its 'hunter and bow' story is its own rendering from Latin/Greek (not public-domain English): do not use it on the page, or mark it 'Our translation'.
People who search 'St Anthony prayer' mean Anthony of Padua. The page should say in one line that this is a different saint.

items.text: No monk yet knew the far desert; those who wished to live apart did so near their own village. Antony copied an old man in the next village who had lived as a hermit from his youth. He sought out every good man he heard of, "like the prudent bee", noting the graciousness of one, the prayer of another, another's freedom from anger, and strove to unite the qualities of each.
items.note: Exact: 'like the prudent bee, he went forth and sought him'.

items.text: On his way to the mountain he passed real gold scattered in the road, at a run.
items.source: Life of Antony, chapter 12 (the silver dish is chapter 11)
items.note: The fort was 'so long deserted that it was full of creeping things'.

items.text: Those who were healed were taught to thank God, not Antony; he did not boast when heard, nor murmur when not.
items.note: Exact: 'those who were healed were taught not to give thanks to Antony but to God alone'.

items.text: In Alexandria in 338, pagans and their priests came into the church asking to see "the man of God"; as many became Christians in those few days as in a year. When some tried to keep the crowds off him, he said there were no more of them than of the demons he wrestled on the mountain.
items.note: Chapter 71's 'we' who saw him to the gate is only probably Athanasius (NPNF footnote 1119: 'seems to imply'), so the page does not say Athanasius walked him out.

items.text: To two Greek philosophers, through an interpreter: 'If you came to a foolish man, your labour is superfluous; but if you think me prudent become as I am, for we ought to imitate what is good. And if I had come to you I should have imitated you; but if you to me, become as I am, for I am a Christian.'
At the last visit to the outer mountain he spoke joyously, 'as though sailing from a foreign city to his own'.
At the end of his life his eyes were sound and he had not lost one tooth, though they were worn to the gums.
items.note: Exact: 'of his teeth he had not lost one, but they had become worn to the gums through the great age of the old man'. Printed in 'In numbers' as Teeth lost 0.

items.text: Robertson, the editor, on Antony's character: 'We see nothing but tenderness and love of men in his character'. He found some stories 'indescribably silly' but concluded that 'overwhelming probability' is against those who denied Athanasius wrote the Life.
items.note: The sentence goes on to call Shenoute ('Senuti') a fanatic; the page stops at 'character'.

items.text: The philosopher's question to Antony: 'How can you endure, father, being deprived of the comfort of books?'
items.source: Socrates, Church History, Book 4, chapter 23 (quoting Evagrius)

items.text: The visitor who told Augustine about Antony was Pontitianus, an African at the emperor's court. Augustine then wept under a fig tree before opening Paul's letters.

Paul the Simple was sixty; Antony shut the door on him for three days, then set him to weave palm-leaf mats and to unpick and reweave them; Paul neither murmured nor was angry, and Antony made him a monk.

Antony to Didymus, in full: 'I am surprised that a wise man should grieve at the loss of a faculty which he shares with ants and flies and gnats, and not rejoice rather in having one of which only saints and apostles have been thought worthy.'
